What happens if the SwMI cannot provide the QoS requested during PDP context activation?

If the SwMI is unable to provide the requested QoS, it may offer an alternative QoS which the MS may accept or reject. If the MS accepts the offered QoS, SNDCP reports the agreed QoS to the application that requested the PDP context activation.
Under what condition is the MS SNDCP permitted to attempt re-negotiation of the QoS for an activated PDP context?
The MS SNDCP is permitted to attempt re-negotiation when the application’s QoS requirements change.
What action does the MS SNDCP take when the SwMI informs it that the QoS of an activated PDP context has been altered?
The MS SNDCP informs the applications that are using the affected PDP context.
What information may the MS include when requesting activation of a secondary PDP context regarding QoS filtering?

The MS may include 'QoS filter' information indicating a port number or a range of port numbers appropriate to that PDP context, or specifically request that the SwMI generates and uses an automatic QoS filter.
How can the MS subsequently modify the QoS filter of an activated PDP context?

The MS can request that the SwMI adds the specified new QoS filter to the existing QoS filter, replaces the existing QoS filter with the new QoS filter, or removes the specified items from the existing QoS filter.
How should the SwMI handle a request from the MS to add a QoS filter to a PDP context if the SwMI is currently using an automatic QoS filter?
The SwMI should combine the newly requested QoS filter with the automatic QoS filter and use the new combined QoS filter with that PDP context.
What action must the SwMI take regarding its automatic QoS filter when it receives a request from the MS to replace the QoS filter for a PDP context?
The SwMI should stop using that automatic QoS filter and use the new QoS filter.
Why might an MS request the removal of a port number or range from the QoS filter for a PDP context?
This could be useful if the MS wishes the SwMI to use the related primary PDP context for those port number(s).
What happens if QoS was not negotiated during PDP context activation?
If QoS was not negotiated during PDP context activation, the background class is assumed, which results in the assignment of an acknowledged advanced link.
What is the consequence for a recently designed MS that does not negotiate QoS when using an SwMI conforming to ETSI EN 300 392-2 V3.4.1 or earlier?
The MS will be unable to access D8PSK and QAM channels.
What is the function of the READY timer and what happens when it expires following inactivity?
The READY timer controls the time the MS stays on a PDCH. When it expires following inactivity, the MS is normally returned to the common control channel.
What is the function of a CONTEXT_READY timer in an MS?
A CONTEXT_READY timer is an inactivity timer for a specific PDP context, with one timer used per PDP context.
Under what condition is the use of CONTEXT_READY timers required for an MS?
The use of CONTEXT_READY timers is required for an MS that supports the transmission or reception of data through more than one PDP context at the same time.
Which IETF RFCs for header and data compression are currently supported by TETRA?
TETRA supports TCP/IP header compression (IETF RFC 1144), IP header compression (IETF RFC 2507 and IETF RFC 2508), BSD compression (IETF RFC 1977), and predictor compression (IETF RFC 1978).
What is the function of the data priority facility in SNDCP?
The data priority facility enables the MS to indicate a priority for obtaining access to radio resource, both for achieving access to a PDCH and for receiving slot grants on the PDCH.
How does SNDCP determine the "MS default data priority"?
SNDCP determines the "MS default data priority" by inspecting the data priority requirements of PDP contexts that are actively transmitting or receiving data.
What action does SNDCP take if the determined "MS default data priority" differs from the "network default data priority" indicated by the SwMI?
SNDCP negotiates the "MS default data priority" with the SwMI.
Why does SNDCP advise layer 2 of short-term variations in the data priority of individual data packets?
So that layer 2 can indicate a priority for obtaining reserved slots.
What information does the MS indicate to the SwMI when requesting access to a PDCH, and what is the purpose?
The MS indicates the highest data priority of any pending data packets to the SwMI, so that the MS can be sent to the PDCH ahead of other MSs with lower data priority.
What are the two options for the MS SNDCP regarding layer 2 advanced links on the new cell after receiving a response PDU from the SwMI SNDCP entity?
The MS SNDCP either requests layer 2 to re-establish the relevant advanced link(s) on the new cell, or requests layer 2 to reconnect the relevant advanced link(s) on the new cell.
What is advanced link roaming and what are its benefits when supported by both MS and SwMI?

Advanced link roaming is method b, where the MS requests layer 2 to reconnect the relevant advanced link(s). It allows the MS to continue using the advanced link on the new cell with all parameters, variables, and timers carried over from the previous cell without loss of data, enabling continuation of transmission or reception from where it finished on the previous cell.
What are the two sublayers that comprise the data link layer?
The data link layer comprises the Logical Link Control (LLC) entity and the Medium Access Control (MAC) entity.
Which specific functions are performed by the lower MAC sublayer?
The lower MAC performs channel coding, interleaving, and scrambling.
What are the main functionalities of the MAC entity?
The main functionalities of the MAC are channel access control, radio resource control, data transfer, link adaptation on a D8PSK or QAM channel, and air interface encryption when required.
How does U-plane traffic enter the MAC layer and is LLC functionality applied to it?

U-plane traffic, end-to-end user signalling, and encryption synchronization information enter the MAC directly from the U-plane application through the TMD-SAP. No LLC functionality applies for U-plane information.
Where does the separation of C-plane and U-plane information occur in the protocol stack?
The separation of C-plane and U-plane information takes place above the MAC layer.
How do Base Stations (BSs) and Mobile Stations (MSs) utilize downlink and uplink frequencies in TETRA?
In TETRA, BSs transmit on downlink frequencies and receive on uplink frequencies, while MSs transmit on uplink frequencies and receive on downlink frequencies.
What is the relationship between downlink and uplink RF carriers in terms of pairing and separation?
A downlink and uplink are paired together on two RF carriers, and each downlink RF carrier and its corresponding uplink RF carrier are separated by the duplex spacing.
Which timeslot and frames does the Main Control CHannel (MCCH) occupy in a Conventional Access (CA) cell during normal operation?
In the normal mode of operation, the MCCH occupies timeslot 1 of the CA main carrier in all frames 1 to 18.
How does a Base Station indicate the number of common secondary control channels (SCCHs) in operation, and how does an MS determine which channel to use?

The BS uses an information element in a broadcast message (the SYSINFO PDU) to indicate the number of common SCCHs currently in operation. The MS calculates which common control channel to use from a parameter received on registration or at subscription.
What are the modulation type and slot capacity for MCCH and common SCCHs on a CA cell?
On a CA cell, the MCCH and any common SCCHs each occupy only one slot capacity on the main carrier and are always π/4-DQPSK channels.
Which timeslots on the main carrier are occupied by the first, second, and third common SCCHs in a CA cell when they are in operation?
The first common SCCH occupies timeslot 2, the second common SCCH occupies timeslot 3, and the third common SCCH occupies timeslot 4 of the main carrier.
Under what condition does a CA MS stop receiving a π/4-DQPSK common control channel?
A CA MS stops receiving a π/4-DQPSK common control channel when it is directed by the BS to an assigned channel, which is assigned for a circuit mode call or for secondary control.
What are the possible bandwidths for the DA main carrier frequency in a DA cell?
The bandwidth of the DA main carrier can be 25 kHz, 50 kHz, 100 kHz, or 150 kHz.
How does an MS determine which common control channel to use when common SCCHs are in operation?
The MS calculates which common control channel to use from a parameter that it received on registration or at subscription.
Which timeslots on the DA main carrier are occupied by a three-slot MCCH-Q?
A three-slot MCCH-Q occupies timeslots 1, 2 and 3 of the DA main carrier.
Can a BS use QAM common SCCHs while using a multi-slot MCCH-Q?
No, the BS cannot use QAM common SCCH(s) if it is using a multi-slot MCCH-Q.
What determines whether an MS acts as a CA MS or a DA MS when it is both CA-capable and DA-capable?
It depends on whether its current serving cell is a CA cell or a DA cell.
How are phase modulation carriers and QAM carriers defined based on the channels they carry?
A phase modulation carrier is one currently carrying π/4-DQPSK and/or D8PSK channels, while a QAM carrier is one currently carrying QAM channels.
Under what condition does an MS receive MCCH, MCCH-Q, or common SCCH instead of being directed to an assigned channel?
An MS receives these channels unless the BS sends a channel allocation message addressed to that MS (individually or to one of its group addresses) directing it to an assigned channel.
What distinguishes the availability of SACCH from FACCH on an assigned traffic channel?
SACCH is available only in frame 18, whereas FACCH is available in all frames 1 to 18, depending on whether the assigned channel in that direction is carrying traffic.
Under what conditions may the BS permit the MS to use timeslot 1 as a Carrier Specific Signalling (CSS) channel?
The BS may permit the MS to use timeslot 1 as a CSS channel if the allocated carrier is not the main carrier and the assigned channel is a π/4-DQPSK or D8PSK channel.
What are the two primary purposes for allocating an assigned SCCH?

An assigned SCCH may be allocated to continue control signalling after the initial random access or paging message, or for use as a packet data channel for the exchange of packet data between the BS and MS(s).
How is channel usage scheduled for packet data channels, and under what control do MSs transmit?
For packet data channels, the channel usage of both downlink and uplink is scheduled dynamically by the BS, and MSs transmit only under BS control via random access or reserved access.
What are the RF bandwidth specifications for π/4-DQPSK, D8PSK, and QAM channels?
The RF bandwidth of a π/4-DQPSK or D8PSK channel is 25 kHz. The RF bandwidth of a QAM channel may be 25 kHz, 50 kHz, 100 kHz, or 150 kHz.
Can a Base Station allocate D8PSK and π/4-DQPSK channels on the same RF carrier?
Yes, the BS may allocate D8PSK channel(s) on the same RF carrier as π/4-DQPSK channel(s), provided they are in different timeslots. This can occur on the main carrier or on other carriers.
Is it permissible to allocate a QAM channel on the same carrier as π/4-DQPSK or D8PSK channels?
No, the BS should not allocate a QAM channel on the same carrier as π/4-DQPSK or D8PSK channel(s).
How are MCCH-Q physical channels utilized for MSs camped on a DA cell?

For DA, the BS may allocate MCCH-Q physical channel(s) as a QAM assigned channel for some MSs camped on the cell. In this configuration, MSs in common mode and MSs in assigned mode share the channel, though they may use slightly different procedures.
What defines a CA MS and a DA MS in terms of their camped cell and received control channels?

A CA MS is an MS currently camped on a CA cell, receiving a π/4-DQPSK common control channel (MCCH or π/4-DQPSK common SCCH) unless directed to an assigned channel. A DA MS is an MS currently camped on a DA cell, receiving a QAM common control channel (MCCH-Q or QAM common SCCH) unless directed to an assigned channel.
Can a channel on a carrier other than the main carrier be shared by both CA MSs and DA MSs?
Yes, a channel on a carrier other than either main carrier might be used as an assigned channel shared by both CA MSs and DA MSs. This applies to both phase modulation carriers and QAM carriers.
Under what condition can a channel on a main carrier be used as an assigned channel shared by CA and DA MSs?
If a channel on either main carrier is not being used for common control, it might be used as an assigned channel shared by both CA MSs and DA MSs.
Which channels can be shared between DA MSs in common mode, DA MSs in assigned mode, and CA MSs in assigned mode?

The MCCH-Q or a QAM common SCCH can be used as an assigned SCCH for CA MSs and also for DA MSs camped on the DA cell, allowing the channel to be shared among DA MSs in common mode, DA MSs in assigned mode, and CA MSs in assigned mode.
Why does the TETRA standard ETSI EN 300 392-2 not support using any channel on a DA main carrier as an assigned channel for MSs camped on a different DA cell?
It is because cell-specific broadcast information needs to be sent on the DA main carrier.
What modulation method is used for all signalling, data messages, and traffic on a π/4-DQPSK channel?
All signalling and data messages and traffic are sent using π/4-DQPSK modulation.
What is the RF bandwidth of both π/4-DQPSK and D8PSK channels?
The RF bandwidth for both channel types is 25 kHz.
How does a receiving MS or BS determine whether a slot contains a π/4-DQPSK burst or a π/8-D8PSK burst on a D8PSK channel?
The receiving device determines the burst type by checking whether the training sequence uses the π/4-DQPSK form or the π/8-D8PSK form.
What are the six valid combinations of modulation level and coding rate for a QAM channel?
The six valid combinations are: 4-QAM with coding rate r=1/2; 16-QAM with coding rate r=1/2 or 1; and 64-QAM with coding rate r=1/2, 2/3, or 1.
Which modulation and coding rate are used for the SICH-Q/D logical channel and Frequency Correction Bursts (FCB) on a QAM downlink?
Both the SICH-Q/D logical channel and Frequency Correction Bursts (FCB) always use 4-QAM with coding rate r=1/2.
How does the RF bandwidth of a QAM channel determine the number of parallel random access uplink RF channel subslots within a single subslot?
A 50 kHz channel provides two parallel subslots, a 100 kHz channel provides four, and a 150 kHz channel provides six parallel random access uplink RF channel subslots within a single subslot.
What modulation and coding rate does the SICH-Q/U logical channel use in the uplink burst?
The SICH-Q/U logical channel always uses 4-QAM with a coding rate of r=1/2.
What is the purpose of the SICH-Q/U channel in an uplink slot or subslot?
It indicates the modulation level and coding rate used in the remainder of that slot or subslot.
What is the timing relationship between uplink and downlink slots in TETRA?
The structure is the same on both uplink and downlink, except that the same-numbered slots on the uplink lag behind the downlink by two slots.
How does the slot arrangement enable a frequency half duplex MS to operate on a single-slot channel?

The slot arrangement allows the MS to receive the downlink slot and transmit in the corresponding (same-numbered) uplink slot. The MS switches between its receive and transmit frequencies in time to perform these actions, enabling time division duplex operation.
What is the timing relationship between the downlink reception and uplink transmission for a single-slot channel occupying timeslot 1 in frame 7?
The BS transmission in frame 7 slot 1 on the downlink is received by the MS. The corresponding uplink transmission occurs in the similarly numbered frame 7 slot 1, which follows two slots later.
What information does the Access Assignment Channel (AACH or AACH-Q) convey?
The Access Assignment Channel contains information about the downlink slot in which it appears, as well as access rights or usage information for the corresponding uplink slot.
In the normal mode of CA operation, which timeslot and frames does the MCCH occupy on the CA main carrier?
The MCCH occupies timeslot 1 of the CA main carrier, in all frames 1 to 18.
Under what condition does a BS enter minimum mode in CA operation?
A BS enters minimum mode when timeslot 1 on the CA main carrier is assigned so that there is no common control channel available in downlink timeslot 1.
What is the maximum number of CA cells that can share an MCCH in MCCH sharing mode?
In MCCH sharing mode, the MCCH may be shared by up to 36 CA cells.
How are downlink MCCH transmissions managed during common frames in MCCH sharing mode?
During common frames, any of the BSs may transmit on the downlink MCCH, but they are scheduled by the infrastructure to avoid use of one slot by multiple BSs.
For which modulation types and how many timeslots does traffic carrier sharing apply between adjacent cells?
Traffic carrier sharing allows the four timeslots of phase modulation carriers other than the main carrier to be shared between up to four adjacent cells for π/4-DQPSK and D8PSK channels.
Can a Base Station allocate uplink and downlink channels for different purposes within the same timeslot?

Yes, a BS may allocate uplink and downlink channels for different purposes, meaning the same timeslot may be allocated for different purposes on the uplink and downlink of that carrier. This applies to both traffic and control channels.
Is the BS allowed to assign different modulation modes, such as π/4-DQPSK for downlink and D8PSK for uplink, to corresponding channels?
No, the BS is not permitted to allocate different modulation modes (i.e. π/4-DQPSK, D8PSK, QAM) for the downlink channel and the corresponding uplink channel.
Under what condition is the basic link available, and how does it relate to the advanced link when the latter is established?
The basic link is available whenever the MS is synchronized to the BS. When an advanced link is established, the basic link remains available.
Besides basic and advanced link PDUs, what other type of PDUs may the LLC send and receive, and what information do they carry?
The LLC may send and receive layer 2 signalling PDUs. These PDUs carry various types of general signalling information relating to layer 2 functions, either LLC or MAC functions.
How does the LLC deliver a PDU to the MAC layer?
The LLC issues the PDU to the MAC as a MAC Service Data Unit (TM-SDU).
What is the MAC's responsibility during random access transmission?
The MAC in the MS is responsible for sending retries until it receives a MAC response from the BS indicating successful random access.
What are the differences between fragmentation and segmentation regarding where they are performed and the link type used?
Fragmentation may be performed in the MAC for the basic link (or for layer 2 signalling), while segmentation may be performed in the LLC for an advanced link.
Under what condition does the LLC use numbered segmentation in the advanced link?
The LLC uses numbered segmentation when the message is too long to be sent in a single MAC block.
What are the possible configurations for simultaneous acknowledged advanced links in an MS?

An MS may have up to four independent acknowledged advanced links. It may use either one original acknowledged advanced link plus up to three extended acknowledged advanced links, or up to four extended acknowledged advanced links.
How are basic links associated with multiple simultaneous advanced links that share the same MAC layer resource?
If multiple simultaneous advanced links share the same resource at the MAC layer, there is only one basic link associated with those advanced links.
Which two elements does the protocol use in the advanced link set-up PDU to indicate the type of resource information?
The protocol uses the elements "Connection width" and "Data transfer throughput" in the advanced link set-up PDU to indicate the type of resource information.
How does an MS request a specific number of phase modulation timeslots per TDMA frame?

The MS requests a specific number of phase modulation timeslots per TDMA frame by setting the "Data transfer throughput" element to a value other than 1102. In this case, other elements indicate the requested radio resources in terms of π/4-DQPSK timeslots.
What is the function of the "Data transfer throughput" element in advanced link resource requests?

The "Data transfer throughput" element indicates how much of the total throughput of the requested radio resources should be available for the advanced link. Maximum throughput is realized when only one MS uses the whole capacity, while lower values indicate that the same radio resources could be used for multiple advanced links for one or more MSs.
How is a request for a phase modulation channel without specifying a number of timeslots per TDMA frame indicated?
It is indicated by setting the "Connection width" element to "1" and the "Data transfer throughput" element to 1102.
When a specified multislot phase modulation connection is requested, what does the information about the number of π/4-DQPSK timeslots per TDMA frame indicate?
It indicates the requested radio resource. The request may be for a symmetric or asymmetric phase modulation advanced link.
Why may segments be of different sizes on a D8PSK channel?
Segments may be of different sizes depending on whether they are cut to be sent using π/4-DQPSK or π/8-D8PSK modulation for the first transmission of that segment.
How is the segment size determined on a 25 kHz or 50 kHz QAM channel?
On a 25 kHz or 50 kHz QAM channel, the segment size is normally determined by the available space in a full-slot MAC block using 4-QAM with coding rate r=1/2 at the current RF bandwidth.
Why is fragmentation needed on a D8PSK channel when retransmitting a segment cut for π/8-D8PSK transmission using π/4-DQPSK modulation?
Fragmentation is needed because the capacity of a π/8-D8PSK MAC block is greater than the capacity of a π/4-DQPSK MAC block.
How is the segment size determined for a 25 kHz or 50 kHz QAM channel to enable retransmission without fragmentation?
The segment size corresponds to the smallest full-slot MAC block size, which is defined as 4-QAM with a coding rate of r = 1/2.
If four segments sent in a full slot using 64-QAM with coding rate r = 2/3 fail to decode, how can they be retransmitted using 16-QAM?
The four failed segments can be retransmitted in two slots using 16-QAM with a coding rate of r = 1/2, placing two segments in each slot.
What are the potential consequences or actions required after a reduction of RF bandwidth, such as changing from 50 kHz to 25 kHz?
Fragmentation may be needed for retransmissions of segments cut for transmission on the old channel, or alternatively, the advanced link may be reset.
How does the segment size determination differ for a 100 kHz or 150 kHz QAM channel compared to a 25 kHz or 50 kHz channel?

For a 100 kHz or 150 kHz QAM channel, the segment size corresponds to half the size of the smallest full-slot MAC block, whereas for 25 kHz or 50 kHz channels, it corresponds to the full smallest full-slot MAC block size.
When does the LLC construct and issue a layer 2 signalling PDU to the MAC?

The LLC constructs the layer 2 signalling PDU and issues it to the MAC via the TMA-SAP when the MAC indicates that it is ready to send a message, such as when it is ready to perform random access or has been granted a reserved slot.
What is the procedure for the MAC to receive layer 2 signalling information via the LLC?

The MAC delivers a received TM-SDU to the LLC via the TMA-SAP. If the received LLC PDU is a layer 2 signalling PDU corresponding to a MAC function, the LLC delivers the information to the MAC via the TLE-SAP.
Why was the decision made to use LLC PDUs for sending information corresponding to some MAC functions?
The decision was originally made because of a shortage of available MAC PDU types.
Which functions are covered in clauses 7.5 to 7.10?
Clauses 7.5 to 7.10 cover link adaptation on a D8PSK or QAM channel, energy economy and napping, data priority, scheduled access, cell and channel selection, and circuit mode calls.
What layers are involved in the functions described in clauses 7.5 to 7.10?
The functions involve procedures performed by multiple layers, including the MAC.
How does an MS receive downlink control channels when on a single-slot common control channel?

When on a single-slot common control channel (the MCCH, a single-slot MCCH-Q, or a common SCCH), the MS attempts to receive and decode the appropriate downlink slot on the main carrier in all frames 1 to 18, except when energy economy or dual watch mode and cell reselection procedures take precedence.
What exceptions apply to downlink reception on a multi-slot MCCH-Q?
For a multi-slot MCCH-Q, energy economy, dual watch or part-time reception mode, cell reselection procedures, and linearization and transmission requirements may take precedence over reception.
Under what conditions may an MS have reduced reception requirements?

Reduced reception requirements may occur when the MS is transmitting in traffic mode on an assigned channel in use for traffic, and also for reception in frame 18 when the MS is receiving in traffic mode on a multi-slot channel.
What types of messages does the MAC in the MS look for and process?

The MAC in the MS looks for and processes downlink messages addressed to that individual MS or to one of its valid group addresses, broadcast signalling messages, and the content of the access assignment channel.
Why does reserved access enable higher channel throughput compared to random access?
Reserved access enables higher channel throughput because there are no collisions of messages from different MSs in reserved slots, so the only errors are those caused by propagation problems.
When is the random access protocol generally needed for an MS?
The random access protocol is generally needed when the MS sends a message to initiate a call or transaction.
How does the MAC handle acknowledgements and retransmissions in non-contentious transmission versus random access?

In non-contentious transmission, the MAC provides an unacknowledged signalling service; it transmits the TM-SDU once and informs the LLC when sent, while the LLC controls acknowledgements and retransmissions. In random access, the MAC in the MS is responsible for sending retries until it receives a MAC response from the BS indicating successful random access.
What are the bit lengths and uniqueness scopes of TETRA Subscriber Identity (TSI) and Short Subscriber Identity (SSI)?
The TETRA Subscriber Identity (TSI) is 48 bits long and unique across the complete TETRA domain. The Short Subscriber Identity (SSI) is 24 bits long and unique within one TETRA network.
How is the Short Subscriber Identity (SSI) derived from the TETRA Subscriber Identity (TSI), and what components make up the Mobile Network Identity (MNI)?
The SSI is formed from a TSI by removing the Mobile Network Identity (MNI). The MNI comprises the 10-bit Mobile Country Code (MCC) and the 14-bit Mobile Network Code (MNC).
What components make up a family of TETRA Subscriber Identities (TSI) in an MS?
Each family contains one Individual TETRA Subscriber Identity (ITSI), and may have an Alias TETRA Subscriber Identity (ATSI) and some Group TETRA Subscriber Identities (GTSIs).
Under what conditions is an Alias TETRA Subscriber Identity (ATSI) allocated?
An ATSI is allocated by the SwMI when an MS visits a network other than its home network; it may also be allocated on the home network to support secure network operations.
What are the components of the TETRA Equipment Identity (TEI) and who allocates it?
The TEI contains a Type Approval Code, Final Assembly Code, Electronic Serial Number and spare digit. It is allocated by the equipment manufacturer.
What determines whether the layer 2 address in a MAC PDU is a source or destination address?
The layer 2 address is the source address for an uplink PDU and the destination address for a downlink PDU.
Which specific identifiers can serve as the address in a MAC PDU?
The address in a MAC PDU can be a Short Subscriber Identity (ISSI, ASSI or GSSI), a USSI, an SMI, or a 10-bit event label.
How does the MAC in the MS handle a received PDU that is addressed to itself?
If the PDU is addressed to itself, the MAC processes the PDU and passes the TM-SDU to the LLC.
What is the primary intended use case for event label assignment, and what specific benefit does it provide on a packet data channel?

Event label assignment is primarily intended for when an advanced link or advanced links have been set up for the appropriate address. On a packet data channel, its use reduces the address size by 14 bits, allowing each LLC data segment to carry 14 bits more user data.
Which MAC PDUs require the use of an event label, and how many bits do they save per data segment on the uplink and downlink?

MAC-U-BLCK on the uplink and MAC-D-BLCK on the downlink can only be used with an event label. Their use saves a further four bits per data segment on the uplink and 11 or 12 bits per data segment on the downlink.
How does the random access protocol usage differ between unsolicited MS messages and messages solicited by the BS?
The random access protocol is generally used for unsolicited MS messages, whereas messages solicited by the BS are generally sent in a subslot or slot(s) reserved by the BS for that MS.
What is a subscriber class and at which levels is it used for control?
A subscriber class is a subdivision of the subscriber population. It is used at the MLE level for controlling which MSs are allowed to use a cell, and at the MAC level for random access control.
How many subscriber classes can an MS belong to, and when does it receive this membership information?
An MS may belong to more than one of the 16 subscriber classes. It receives its subscriber class membership information on registration or at subscription.
Under what condition is random access to the system permitted for an MS?
Random access to the system is only permitted when invited by the BS. An MS wishing to access must wait until an access opportunity is presented by the BS, as indicated in the downlink signalling.
Under what conditions may an MS use a subslot designated for a particular access code?
An MS may use the subslot only if the PDU priority, and the subscriber class parameter or MS identity, conform to the current binding.
On which channels and slots is the ACCESS-ASSIGN PDU normally transmitted?

The ACCESS-ASSIGN PDU is transmitted in every downlink slot of a π/4-DQPSK or D8PSK channel on the AACH. It is also normally transmitted in downlink slots of a QAM channel (except slots containing BS linearization) on the AACH-Q.
What information does the ACCESS-ASSIGN PDU convey regarding uplink timeslots?
It conveys information about the usage of the downlink slot in which it appears, and access rights for the corresponding uplink timeslot, which is two slots later.
Does the ACCESS-ASSIGN PDU include the identity of an MS for which a subslot is reserved?
No, the identity of the MS does not appear in the ACCESS-ASSIGN PDU. The MS is informed separately using a downlink signalling message addressed to that MS.
Which PDUs are contained in the BNCH and BNCH-Q broadcast network channels?
The BNCH channel contains the SYSINFO PDU, while the BNCH-Q channel contains the SYSINFO-Q or SYSINFO-DA PDU.
Under what condition might a Base Station not use the ACCESS-DEFINE PDU?
A Base Station may not use the ACCESS-DEFINE PDU if it does not need multiple access codes, as the facilities provided by the SYSINFO, SYSINFO-Q, and SYSINFO-DA PDUs may be adequate.
How are access requests timed on a 25 kHz channel according to the slotted Aloha principle?
Access requests are made subslot synchronous, meaning they occur in subslot 1 or subslot 2, not partway through a subslot.
How does the ACCESS-ASSIGN PDU define the use of uplink subslots?
The designation is performed using the ACCESS-ASSIGN PDU, with two access fields in the ACCESS-ASSIGN PDU sent in a downlink slot defining the use of the two corresponding uplink subslots.
What must an MS's MAC do if an immediate first access request is not made?

If an immediate first access request is not made, the MS's MAC has to wait for an ACCESS-ASSIGN PDU containing a frame marker for its access code, and then chooses a subslot randomly from that access frame for its first access request.
Who decides between using rolling access frames and discrete access frames, and does the MS need to know this choice?
The BS makes the choice between rolling and discrete access frames. The MS does not need to know which method the BS intends to use, as its access procedures are compatible with either.
How does the BS indicate ongoing frame continuation when using discrete access frames?
The BS uses the "ongoing frame" value, denoted by *, to indicate ongoing frame continuation.
Why and how does the BS vary the frame-length on the uplink channel?

The BS varies the frame-length to prevent excessive collision of access requests from different MSs and to minimize access delays. Under normal conditions, the frame-length is short. When collision is detected, the BS may increase the frame-length dynamically based on its estimate of backlogged traffic.
How many random access uplink RF channel subslots are provided on a 50 kHz QAM channel?
A 50 kHz QAM channel provides two random access uplink RF channel subslots.
What is the bandwidth used for access requests in all QAM channels?
Access requests are sent within a 25 kHz bandwidth for all QAM channels.
How does an MS select a specific subslot for transmitting an access request when parallel random access uplink RF channel subslots are available?

The MS first uses normal procedures to choose a subslot randomly from an access frame and count to it, regarding parallel subslots as a single subslot. Upon reaching the chosen subslot, the MS makes a random choice of one of the available random access uplink RF channel subslots (two, four, or six) corresponding to that subslot and transmits the access request in the selected one.
What is the benefit of providing parallel random access uplink RF channel subslots?
It enables a higher random access throughput than using the full RF bandwidth of the channel for one access request.
When is the random access protocol generally needed by an MS?
The random access protocol is generally needed when an MS wishes to initiate a call or transaction.
How are subsequent transmissions from an MS handled after random access has been performed?
Subsequent transmissions from the MS can use reserved access, meaning the BS can schedule the MS transmissions into specified uplink slots.
What information does the ACCESS-ASSIGN PDU sent by the BS indicate?
The ACCESS-ASSIGN PDU indicates which uplink slots and subslots are reserved and therefore not available for random access by other MSs.
What capability does the multiple slot granting facility on a QAM channel provide?
It allows the BS to grant disjoint resources to an MS with one slot grant.
What information does the "basic slot granting" element indicate in a PDU?
The "basic slot granting" element indicates the amount of reserved capacity (a single subslot or one or more full slots) and the time delay until the start of the reservation.
How does multiple slot granting enable the BS to grant disjoint resources with one slot grant on a QAM channel?

Multiple slot granting enables the BS to grant disjoint resources with one slot grant by including up to seven explicit instances of the "basic slot granting" element in one slot grant, and/or by using an implicit repeat mechanism for each instance of the "basic slot granting" element, allowing the BS to specify that the MS should behave as if it had received the "basic slot granting" element a number of times (up to 11 times).
What is the primary function of the implicit repeat mechanism in resource allocation?
The implicit repeat mechanism allows a patterned repetition of resources to be granted with one "basic slot granting" element.
In which scenarios is the implicit repeat mechanism particularly useful for allocating resources?

It is useful for allocating resources to an MS using scheduled access with a fairly short schedule repetition period (within the range of the granting time delay), or for allocating resources to other MSs sharing the channel with an MS that is using scheduled access.
How does an implicit repeat count of 9 affect the total number of times a one-slot grant is applied?
An implicit repeat count of 9 means that the one-slot grant applies 10 times.
When is the use of multiple explicit instances of the "basic slot granting" element preferred over the implicit repeat mechanism?
Multiple explicit instances are useful for providing disjoint slot grants that are not based on a patterned repetition of resources.
Which specific slots and frames are included in the granted allocation comprising slots 2 and 3 of frame 9, slots 3 and 4 of frame 11, slots 2, 3 and 4 of frame 12, and slot 2 of frame 13?
The granted allocation comprises slots 2 and 3 of frame 9, slots 3 and 4 of frame 11, slots 2, 3 and 4 of frame 12, and slot 2 of frame 13.
In what scenarios is the use of multiple explicit instances of the "basic slot granting" element combined with the implicit repeat mechanism considered useful?
It is useful at the beginning of a patterned repetition of resources or if the BS wishes to regain the exact synchronization of a patterned repetition of resources after a linearization opportunity.

In Example 3 on a four-slot QAM channel, what is the resulting granted allocation when the first basic slot granting element grants one slot with no delay and no implicit repeat, and the second grants one slot with a three-opportunity delay and an implicit repeat count of 8?
The granted allocation comprises slot 4 of each of frames 3 to 12.
How does the BS handle slot granting for an MS transmitting background class data, such as file transfer, in relation to other access types?
The BS uses multiple slot granting to fit the granted slots in the gaps between scheduled access transmissions while leaving space for random access and/or reserved access for other MSs.
What information is included in the basic channel allocation for a π/4-DQPSK channel?

The basic channel allocation for a π/4-DQPSK channel includes information about the type of allocation (e.g., replacement of the current channel or allocation of an additional independent channel for an independent service), the assigned timeslot or timeslots per TDMA frame, and the allocated RF carrier.
Under what conditions does the BS use an augmented channel allocation instead of a basic one?
The BS uses an augmented channel allocation when it wishes to allocate a D8PSK or QAM channel, or if it wishes to permit "napping" on the assigned channel.
What additional information is included in an augmented channel allocation?

An augmented channel allocation includes the RF bandwidth of the allocated channel, the modulation mode (π/4-DQPSK, D8PSK, or QAM), the conforming channel status (conforming, non-conforming concentric, sectored, super-sectored, or eccentric), BS transmit power and BS link imbalance information, and optional napping information.
How is a "concentric channel" defined in terms of its radiation pattern and site?
A concentric channel is defined as a channel that has essentially the same azimuthal radiation pattern as the main carrier and is radiated from the same site as the main carrier.
What defines a non-conforming concentric channel?
A non-conforming concentric channel is a concentric channel that has a larger or smaller range than the main carrier.
How does a sectored channel differ from a super-sectored channel in terms of azimuthal extent?

A sectored channel has an azimuthal extent that is smaller than, and contained entirely within, the azimuthal extent of the main carrier. In contrast, a super-sectored channel has an azimuthal extent that exceeds the azimuthal extent of the main carrier in at least one azimuthal direction.
On which type of channels does closed loop power control apply for the MS?
Closed loop power control applies only on $\pi/4$-DQPSK traffic channels.
What is the default mechanism used by the MS to control its transmit power?
Open loop power control is the default mechanism used by the MS to control its transmit power.
How does the MS calculate its transmitter power for reserved access or traffic transmissions in open loop power control?

The MS subtracts its own measurements of the received BS signal strength from the ACCESS_PARAMETER and uses the result to set its own transmitter power, provided that the result is not greater than the maximum MS power for the channel and not greater than the maximum power that the MS supports.
How is the maximum power modified on wider-bandwidth QAM channels?
On wider-bandwidth QAM channels, the maximum power is modified by a bandwidth factor.
Under what conditions does closed loop power control apply, and on which channels is it used?
Closed loop power control applies only when the MS is transmitting circuit mode traffic and only for the duration of that transmission. It therefore applies only on π/4-DQPSK channels.
How do transmitting entities choose modulation on D8PSK and QAM channels?

On a D8PSK channel, the transmitting MS or BS chooses whether to use a π/4-DQPSK or π/8-D8PSK burst on a slot-by-slot basis. On a QAM channel, the transmitting MS or BS chooses which modulation level and coding rate to use on a slot-by-slot basis, except in the case of random access by the MS and Frequency Correction Bursts sent by the BS.
What factors does the MAC consider when adaptively selecting the bit rate in the link adaptation algorithm?
The MAC selects the appropriate bit rate based on the current link conditions and the "data category" parameter provided by the LLC with the data to be sent.
What is the minimum time period over which an MS or BS is expected to follow changes in link conditions?
It is not expected that the MS or BS would attempt to follow changes in the link conditions over a period shorter than about 0.5 seconds.
How does the MAC of the transmitting MS or BS select the appropriate bit rate when using predefined choices for data categories?
The MAC selects the appropriate bit rate based solely on the "data category" parameter provided by the LLC with the data.
Which factors does the MAC use when selecting the appropriate bit rate?
The MAC uses both the data class and the reliability level when it selects the appropriate bit rate.
On what basis can the MAC choose the bit rate in a simple link adaptation algorithm?
In a simple link adaptation algorithm, the MAC can make its choice of bit rate based solely on the "data category" parameter.
What are the predefined bit rate choices required by ETSI EN 300 392-2 for sending background or telemetry class data on a D8PSK channel?
For background or telemetry class data on a D8PSK channel, the requirement is one transmission of each segment at reliability level 1, using π/8-D8PSK modulation.
Why might an MS decide not to attempt segment transmissions using π/8-D8PSK modulation when channel conditions are poor?

Because fragmentation is generally needed when a segment first sent using π/8-D8PSK is retransmitted using π/4-DQPSK, which impairs the performance of the π/4-DQPSK retransmission compared to if the segment had been first sent using π/4-DQPSK.
Which modulation and coding rate are used for the first retransmission (reliability level 2) of a segment on a QAM channel?
16-QAM with coding rate 1/2.
How is the segment size determined for 25 kHz or 50 kHz QAM channels to avoid the need for fragmentation during retransmission?
The segment size is chosen to correspond to the smallest full-slot MAC block size, which is defined as 4-QAM with a coding rate of 1/2.
What are the two types of layer 2 signalling messages used in the link adaptation process and their respective functions?

The two messages are: 1) L2-LINK-FEEDBACK-CONTROL, used by the BS to request or terminate link adaptation feedback from the MS; and 2) L2-LINK-FEEDBACK-INFO, used by the BS to send feedback information to the MS, or by the MS to send feedback information to the BS.
What information may L2-LINK-FEEDBACK-INFO messages from the BS provide to assist the MS in choosing a transmission bit rate?

The feedback information may indicate the preferred modulation level and coding rate for QAM for a specified data class. Alternatively, it may provide the BS’s estimate of the signal-to-noise ratio received on the uplink and optionally the BS’s estimate of the channel model and speed.
What sources of information can an MS use when measuring the downlink channel?
When making measurements of the downlink channel, the MS may use information from any downlink slots on the channel, not only those slots containing information addressed to itself.
What methods or choices can an MS use when starting to send advanced link data or if a significant time has elapsed since the last transmission of such data?
The MS could use method c) or use a predefined choice of bit rate.
What options are available to an MS when it starts sending real-time data?
The MS could use method c) or use a predefined bit rate.
What is recommended for a BS regarding link adaptation feedback during the transmission of real-time class data?

It is recommended that the BS requests link adaptation feedback during transmission of real-time class data to an individual MS if the BS wishes to use link adaptation for that data. Similarly, it is recommended that the BS sends link adaptation feedback when the MS is transmitting real-time class data if the BS wishes to enable the MS to use link adaptation for that data.
What are the three methods for reduced reception by MSs and their applicable channels?

The three methods are: 1) Energy economy mode (or dual watch mode with an energy economy group), available on a common control channel (MCCH, MCCH-Q, or common SCCH); 2) Part-time reception procedure, which may apply on a multi-slot MCCH-Q; and 3) A 'napping' facility, available for use on an assigned channel.
What is the primary purpose of the energy economy procedure in TETRA?
The primary purpose is to allow Mobile Stations (MSs) to conserve energy and extend battery life while on a common control channel.
How does a Mobile Station enter energy economy mode in TETRA?

The Mobile Station enters energy economy mode by negotiating with the Base Station. This negotiation occurs via message exchange at the Mobility Management layer, either during the registration process or at any other time.
How does the MAC layer behave for an MS on a single-slot common control channel when not active in a message exchange?
The MS's MAC follows a regular cycle of sleeping for the agreed number of TDMA frames and then receiving the appropriate downlink slot in one TDMA frame.
What is the MAC behavior of an MS when the BS broadcasts that enhanced energy economy is not available and the MS is not active in a message exchange?
The MS's MAC follows a regular cycle of sleeping for the agreed number of TDMA frames and then receiving all downlink slots comprising the multi-slot MCCH-Q in one TDMA frame.
How does an MS that does not support or wish to use enhanced energy economy behave during its sleeping cycle, even if the BS indicates availability?
The MS receives all slots comprising the multi-slot MCCH-Q in the reception TDMA frames.
What are the wake-up frequencies for energy economy groups EG5, EG6, and EG7?
In EG5, the MS wakes up once per multiframe. In EG6, it wakes up once every four multiframes. In EG7, it wakes up only once every 20 multiframes.
What information must the Base Station record to ensure messages are transmitted to a Mobile Station at the appropriate time during energy economy mode?
The Base Station needs to record which energy economy group each Mobile Station is in and which start point was assigned to it.
Under what conditions does the MAC temporarily suspend energy economy mode?

The MAC suspends energy economy mode temporarily when it moves to an assigned channel, when the Mobile Station becomes active in a call or advanced link, when it wishes to send a message, or when it receives a message from the Base Station other than broadcast messages.
How does energy economy mode behave when a Mobile Station changes cell within its registered area?

The Mobile Station may maintain the same energy economy mode and follow the same energy economy pattern after acquiring slot and frame synchronization on the new cell, but it uses the slot, frame, and multiframe numbering of the new cell.
Under what condition does an MS leave energy economy mode, and what is required to re-enter it?
The MS leaves energy economy mode if it leaves the registered area. To re-enter energy economy mode, the MS has to make a new request.
What are the two types of dual watch that an MS may use?
An MS may use either full dual watch or idle dual watch.
What reception capabilities does an MS supporting idle dual watch have when it is in an idle state?
An MS supporting idle dual watch is capable of periodically receiving both the Direct Mode RF carrier and the V+D common control channel when idle.
Why might a BS observe that a dual watching MS is not always able to receive in the agreed slots?

Direct Mode requirements may take precedence over V+D requirements to receive or transmit on the V+D common control channel, causing the MS to transmit and/or receive on the Direct Mode side instead of sleeping.
Under what specific conditions may an MS be unable to receive all slots comprising a multi-slot MCCH-Q?
This may occur if the V+D common control channel is a multi-slot MCCH-Q and the BS does not support enhanced energy economy.
Under what conditions does the part-time reception procedure apply to a DA MS?

The part-time reception procedure applies only when a DA MS is in common mode on a multi-slot MCCH-Q and the BS has broadcast that part-time reception is permitted. It does not apply when the MS is on an assigned channel.
How does a DA MS determine the required reception slot during part-time reception?

The required reception slot is derived from the same parameter that the MS uses to derive its reception slot when common SCCHs are in operation. This parameter is received on registration or at subscription.
What triggers a DA MS to revert from part-time reception to multi-slot operation on a multi-slot MCCH-Q?
When an MS is active on the multi-slot MCCH-Q, it reverts to multi-slot operation.
What are the possible configurations for 'napping reception frames' in napping information?

The 'napping reception frames' can be configured as: all downlink TDMA frames; every two TDMA frames (requiring reception in either odd-numbered or even-numbered frames); or every three TDMA frames (requiring reception in every third frame).
What components comprise the napping information provided by the BS?

Napping information comprises: the 'napping reception frames', the 'napping reception timeslots' (a timeslot bit map), the value of the napping inactivity timer, and a flag indicating whether the MS may use reduced reception in frame 18 when not in napping mode.
What is the purpose of the napping method regarding transmission gaps?

The napping method allows the MS to use napping mode (perform reduced reception) during long gaps between transmissions on a packet data channel when the MS has not sent or received a message recently, based on the napping inactivity timer.
On which channel types is the use of the immediate napping permission facility restricted?
The use of the immediate napping permission facility is restricted on $\pi / 4$-DQPSK channels and when using $\pi / 4$-DQPSK modulation on D8PSK channels.
What factors does the BS consider when choosing whether to allow napping on an assigned channel?

The BS considers a compromise between allowing flexibility of scheduling of the downlink channel and providing opportunities for MS neighbour cell monitoring, irregular channel monitoring, main carrier monitoring, background scanning, and/or battery economy. It also considers the preferred reception pattern during short gaps in transmission versus longer gaps between transmissions.
How does the BS manage the 'immediate napping permission flag' when sending background class data to an MS?

The BS may set the 'immediate napping permission flag' to 0 until the end of the data, except during intervals when it knows it will transmit to other MSs. The MS returns to napping mode at the end of the data either immediately or after the inactivity timer expires, depending on the flag setting.
What determines the BS's choice of setting the 'immediate napping permission flag' to 0 or 1 when an MS is sending background class data?
The choice depends on whether the BS needs flexibility to send acknowledgements and slot grants in any slot of the downlink assigned channel.
Under what conditions does the BS set the "immediate napping permission flag" to 1 in downlink MAC PDUs when sending data?

The BS may set the flag to 1 in most or all downlink MAC PDUs when sending data involving intermittent transmissions of short packets, such as real-time class data or telemetry class data. For packets requiring more than one slot, the flag is set to 1 only in the last of the slots sent to the MS.
Which downlink MAC PDUs might contain the "immediate napping permission flag" set to 1 when the MS is sending intermittent short packet data?
When the MS is sending such data, the BS may set the flag to 1 in most or all downlink MAC PDUs sent to the MS, for example, those containing slot grants and/or link adaptation feedback messages.
How does the data priority facility affect slot granting among multiple MSs on the same channel?
It enables the BS to grant slots to an MS with high data-priority PDUs to send ahead of other MSs with lower data-priority PDUs on the same channel.
How many defined values of data priority exist, and how does the BS indicate support for this feature?

There are eight defined values of data priority, plus an "undefined" value. The BS indicates support of data priority using a bit in a broadcast message, specifically SYSINFO, SYSINFO-Q, or SYSINFO-DA PDU.
How does data priority differ from PDU priority in terms of their effects on the MS and BS?

PDU priority affects the MS's queue re-ordering in the LLC and the MS's random access procedure. Data priority principally affects the speed of the MS's access to the packet data channel and the BS's criteria for slot granting on a shared packet data channel, but is also used for queue re-ordering in the LLC.
How does the SNDCP in an MS determine the MS default data priority in relation to the network default data priority?

The SNDCP in an MS chooses a preferred default data priority by inspecting the data priority requirements of actively transmitting or receiving PDP contexts. If this differs from the network default data priority, the SNDCP negotiates a specific MS default data priority with the BS; otherwise, it regards the MS default data priority as being the network default data priority.
What is the role of the MS default data priority in slot granting on a packet data channel?

The MS default data priority is applied by the BS by default to all requirements for reserved slots indicated by that MS on a packet data channel, unless temporarily overridden by a short-term data priority requested by the MS's MAC.
How does the SNDCP in the MS communicate data priority for each packet data PDU to the lower layers?
The SNDCP includes the data priority for that PDU within the request primitive issued to the lower layers.
What is the two-step ordering process used by the LLC for packet data SDUs on a channel?
First, the LLC orders the packet data SDUs according to the PDU priority. Second, it orders the packet data SDUs within one PDU priority according to the data priority.
What are the two possible contents of the data priority layer 2 signalling message sent by the MAC to the BS?
The message may contain either a single short-term data priority (the maximum data priority for the data in the LLC queue for that channel) or up to seven data priority blocks.
What information is included in the data priority block regarding slot requirements?

The data priority block includes the expected number of slots needed to send the currently queued data at that data priority, followed by the residual data priority which applies to slots following those included in the data priority block(s).
Why should MS designers avoid excessive use of data priority layer 2 signalling messages?
Excessive use of data priority layer 2 signalling messages may actually reduce the MS's overall data throughput.
How should the required number of slots at each data priority be treated to balance signaling overhead and capacity needs?

The precise details of the required number of slots at each data priority should be regarded as a snapshot of the current requirements, to be updated at intervals, without the MAC necessarily attempting to update its data priority requirements whenever the LLC has new data to send unless there is an increase in the required data priority.
Under what condition must the MAC update its data priority requirements when the LLC has new data to send?
The MAC must update its data priority requirements when there is an increase in the required data priority.
How does indicating reservation requirements in the reserved access procedure affect the amount of packet data carried in an uplink slot?
The MAC PDU structure allows the reservation requirement to be included in each uplink slot without affecting the amount of packet data that can be carried in the slot.
When does the MS default data priority apply instead of the data priority information sent by the MAC?

The MS default data priority applies after a timer has expired since the MS last sent a data priority layer 2 signalling message, or when the MS initiates the random access procedure on the channel (unless the random access request carries a data priority layer 2 signalling message).
What factors should the BS consider when deciding when to grant reserved slots to MSs on a shared channel?

The BS should use information about the default data priority, short-term data priority information received in data priority layer 2 signalling messages, and may also use uplink fragmentation as a criterion.
Why might the BS's estimate of reserved slots be incorrect on a D8PSK or QAM channel?
The estimate may be incorrect because of the MS's use of link adaptation. The MS indicates its precise requirement when it transmits in the reserved slot(s).
How does multiple slot granting allow the BS to allocate disjoint resources on a QAM channel?

It allows the BS to grant disjoint resources with one slot grant by including multiple explicit instances of the "basic slot granting" element and/or by using an implicit repeat mechanism for each instance of the "basic slot granting" element.
In what scenarios is multiple slot granting considered useful?

It is useful for allocating resources to an MS using scheduled access with a fairly short schedule repetition period, or for allocating resources to other MSs sharing the channel with an MS that is using scheduled access.
Under what conditions should the BS re-start slot grants for a PDP context after pausing them?
The BS should re-start the slot grants if its SNDCP entity receives a data packet from the MS for that PDP context.
Under what conditions should the SwMI inform the MS about alterations to the QoS of an activated PDP context?

The SwMI should inform the MS if it is suspending a schedule because it can no longer provide sufficient resources, if it is able to support a suspended schedule again, or if it is cancelling a schedule to permanently reallocate the scheduled resource.
When must the BS stop sending slot grants appropriate to a schedule?
The BS should stop sending slot grants if the PDP context containing the schedule is deactivated, or if the schedule is suspended or cancelled.
How does the SNDCP in the MS indicate the scheduling status of packet data to the lower layers?
The SNDCP includes a parameter in the request primitive to indicate whether the data should be treated as "not scheduled data", "initial scheduled data" or "scheduled data".
How does the MAC treat initial scheduled data when it has no reserved capacity and has not requested any?
The MAC treats initial scheduled data as "unscheduled", allowing it to immediately use random access to send the data.
How is scheduled data generally handled by the MAC regarding slot grants and random access?
Scheduled data is treated as "fully scheduled" (except for segment retransmissions), so the MAC generally waits for a slot grant instead of attempting random access.
What is the primary responsibility of the MAC in the MS regarding schedule timing?
The MAC in the MS is responsible for maintaining the MS schedule timing.
Under what condition does the MAC in the MS base the timing of further schedule timing prompts on synchronization defined by the BS?
The MAC bases the timing on BS-defined synchronization when the BS sends a layer 2 signalling message to define the schedule synchronization.
What potential issue arises if the BS does not use the schedule synchronization message and the MS has other data to send?
The MS may send its scheduled data with other data before the reserved slots intended for the scheduled data, potentially resulting in no data being available to send in those reserved slots.
How does the MLE make decisions on cell and channel selection and reselection?
The MLE makes these decisions using threshold comparisons based on measurements made by the MS MAC.
What is the distinction between autonomous and requested measurements performed by the MAC?

The MAC autonomously makes measurements on the current channel(s) on the serving cell and passes the results to the MLE. It makes other measurements on selected neighbouring cells or on selected channels on the serving cell only upon specific request from the MLE.
What are the reliability requirements for the initial cell selection procedure?
The procedure must ensure that the MS selects a cell where it can reliably decode downlink data on the main carrier and has a high probability of uplink communication.
What steps does the MS MLE take during initial cell selection to identify and choose a cell?

The MS MLE initiates the MAC's foreground scanning procedure to measure signal levels on various cells. It uses these results to produce and rank a list of preferred cells. The MS then selects the highest-ranked cell if its main carrier radio connection is of adequate quality and performs registration if needed.
Under what conditions does the MS continue scanning for cells during initial selection?
If none of the measured cells is suitable, the MS continues scanning until a suitable cell is found or until the MS is powered down.
What criteria trigger cell reselection decisions by the MS MLE?

Cell reselection is triggered if the radio link on the serving cell has failed, or if the quality of the serving cell's main carrier radio connection falls below a certain level and the quality of a neighbour cell exceeds that of the serving cell by a certain amount.
Under what conditions may the MLE perform cell reselection irrespective of the serving cell's link quality?

The MLE may perform cell reselection irrespective of the serving cell's link quality if the service provided by a neighbour cell is higher than that provided by the serving cell, and the neighbour cell has a main carrier radio connection of sufficient quality (i.e., the neighbour cell is "radio usable").
In which MS modes can the MLE perform cell reselection, and what are the five categories it handles?

The MLE can perform cell reselection when the MS is attached to a cell in idle or traffic mode. The procedure handles five categories: undeclared, unannounced, announced type 3, announced type 2, and announced type 1.
When is undeclared cell reselection used, and what actions may the MS take afterwards?

Undeclared cell reselection is used when the MS is not currently involved in any voice or circuit mode data calls. After the cell reselection, the MS may attempt to recover SNDCP and/or advanced link connections on the new cell.
What distinguishes unannounced from announced cell reselection regarding MS notification and connection recovery?

Unannounced cell reselection is used when the MS is unable to or has no need to inform the serving cell of its intention to find service on another cell prior to reselection; the MS may attempt to recover CMCE and SNDCP and/or advanced link connections on the new cell. Announced cell reselection is used when the MS informs the serving cell prior to the cell change and attempts to restore the call(s) upon arrival at the new serving cell, which maximizes the probability of restoring CMCE and SNDCP connections.
What characterizes Type 3 reselection for MSs unable to perform background scanning?

Type 3 reselection requires the MS to break calls temporarily to perform foreground scanning for broadcast and synchronization information. After selecting the new cell, call restoration signalling may be used to restore the calls.
How does Type 2 reselection differ from Type 1 regarding SwMI direction and MS actions?

In Type 2 reselection, the SwMI does not direct the MS to a channel in the new cell. The MS selects the MCCH or MCCH-Q on the new cell, performs call restoration signalling, and may then be allocated a traffic channel. In contrast, Type 1 allows the SwMI to direct the MS, and no call restoration signalling is required from the MS.
Under what conditions is Type 1 reselection applicable and what role does the SwMI play?

Type 1 reselection requires that the MS has performed background scanning (and received a SYSINFO-DA PDU if the selected cell is a DA cell) and that the SwMI can direct the MS from the original traffic channel to the MCCH/MCCH-Q or directly to a traffic channel on the new cell. If directed to MCCH/MCCH-Q, the SwMI may later allocate a traffic channel.
Who determines whether type 1 or type 2 cell reselection is applied?
The SwMI, not the MS, determines whether type 1 or type 2 cell reselection is to be applied.
What does the MS include in the cell reselection request?
The MS includes the cell to which it intends to move in the cell reselection request.
Under what conditions does the MS include a forward registration request with the cell reselection request?
The MS includes a forward registration request if it is required to register on the new cell and both the MS and the SwMI support forward registration.
What information does the SYNC-DA PDU contain when scanning a DA neighbour cell?
The SYNC-DA PDU contains all the essential information needed for the MS to decide whether it wishes to use the cell.
Under what condition must an MS support type 1 and/or type 2 cell reselection?
If the SwMI provides broadcast of neighbour cell information, the MS has to support type 1 and/or type 2 cell reselection to those cells included in the neighbour cell information.
What are the characteristics of a sectored channel?

A sectored channel has an azimuthal extent that is smaller than, and contained entirely within, the azimuthal extent of the main carrier. It is radiated from the same site as the main carrier and provides a method of extending the range of high RF-bandwidth channels.
How does a semi-super-sectored channel differ from a fully super-sectored channel?

Both are radiated from the same site as the main carrier. A semi-super-sectored channel exceeds the main carrier's azimuthal extent in one direction but is less in the other. A fully super-sectored channel has an azimuthal extent that is greater than, and entirely contains, the azimuthal extent of the main carrier.
What distinguishes an eccentric channel from other channel types described?
An eccentric channel is defined by not being radiated from the same site as the main carrier.
Why was the 4 km separation limit chosen for eccentric channels in the TETRA standard?

It was chosen based on the expectation that existing MSs could tolerate this delay separation, as they already possess tolerance in channel timing to cope with channels having long delay spreads, thereby ensuring backwards compatibility with current MS capabilities.
What defines an "umbrella channel" and which channel types can serve this role?

An umbrella channel is an assignable channel that fully covers the areas of multiple cells. It can be a concentric channel, a fully super-sectored channel, or an eccentric channel, provided each fully covers the radial extent or areas of all its associated cells.
How is a "channel class" defined and how does an MS use it to predict performance?

A channel class is defined as a set of values indicating the general RF characteristics of a concentric channel or fully super-sectored channel. An MS predicts the performance of corresponding channels by using measurements made on another carrier on that cell together with the characteristics of the channel class.
What is the definition of an irregular channel?
An irregular channel is a non-conforming channel that needs to be monitored by the MS in order for the MS to discover whether the channel would be usable as an assigned channel.
How does an MS determine if an irregular channel is usable as an assigned channel?

The MS discovers which irregular channels would be usable as an assigned channel by monitoring each irregular carrier, as it cannot predict their performance by measurements made on any other channel.
Which specific channel types are classified as irregular channels?
Sectored channels and semi-super-sectored channels are irregular channels. An eccentric channel is also an irregular channel if it does not fully cover the area of the cell.
Under what condition might the SwMI broadcast information about a fully super-sectored channel as an irregular channel?

The SwMI may broadcast information about a fully super-sectored channel as an irregular channel if broadcast is needed, for example, if the channel does not fully cover the area of the cell (i.e., if the radial range of the channel is less than the radial range of the main carrier).
How does the MS predict the performance of concentric channels?
The MS predicts the performance of concentric channel(s) from measurements made on another carrier on that cell.
Can the MS predict sectored channel performance using measurements from other channels?
No, the MS cannot predict the performance of a sectored channel by measurements made on any other channel; it discovers which sectored channels it can use by monitoring each sectored carrier.
What defines a concentric channel when the main carrier uses sectored antennas and has a non-circular coverage area?

A concentric channel is defined as a channel radiated from the same site as the main carrier with essentially the same azimuthal radiation pattern, even if the coverage area is not circular. It may have a larger or smaller range and coverage area than the main carrier.
How does a conforming channel differ from a general concentric channel?
A conforming channel is a specific type of concentric channel that has essentially the same range and coverage area as the main carrier.
What distinguishes a sectored channel from the main carrier in terms of azimuthal extent?
A sectored channel is radiated from the same site as the main carrier but has an azimuthal extent that is smaller than, and contained entirely within, the azimuthal extent of the main carrier.
What characterizes a super-sectored channel relative to the main carrier's azimuthal extent?
A super-sectored channel is radiated from the same site as the main carrier but has an azimuthal extent that exceeds the azimuthal extent of the main carrier in at least one azimuthal direction.
What types of channels are present in Cell B?
Cell B contains a main carrier and other π/4-DQPSK conforming channels, as well as QAM non-conforming concentric channels that have a smaller range than the main carrier.
How do the sectored channels in Cell C relate to the cell's azimuthal extent?
In Cell C, the three QAM sectored channels collectively cover the azimuthal extent of the sectored cell, representing a further subdivision of the already sectored cell.
What are the coverage characteristics of a fully super-sectored channel relative to the main carrier?

A fully super-sectored channel exceeds the azimuthal extent of the main carrier in both directions and has at least the same range as the main carrier, thereby fully encompassing the main carrier's coverage.
What is the purpose of using a fully super-sectored channel as an umbrella channel?
It allows an assigned channel to fully cover the areas of multiple cells, enabling a multi-cell group call to use a single assigned channel throughout all covered cells.
What is a typical use case for an eccentric channel in cellular network coverage?

An eccentric channel is used to provide high-bandwidth QAM coverage to a packet data traffic 'hotspot' in an area that is not at the centre of the cell, such as an area of high population or where packet data traffic is expected to be higher than in other parts of the cell.
In the example of a cell using an eccentric channel, what are the characteristics of the concentric and eccentric QAM channels?

The example features a 150 kHz QAM concentric channel available near the centre of the cell, and a 150 kHz QAM eccentric channel radiated from a different site within the cell to cover a specific area.
When does the SwMI broadcast information for use by MSs?
The SwMI broadcasts various types of information for use by MSs during synchronization and when using the cell.
Which PDUs are contained in the Broadcast Synchronization Channel (BSCH) at the MAC and MLE levels?
The BSCH contains the SYNC PDU at the MAC level and the D-MLE-SYNC PDU at the MLE level.
On which channel types are the PDUs from the Broadcast Network Channel (BNCH) sent, and which mobile stations use them?
These PDUs are sent only on π/4-DQPSK and D8PSK channels. They are used by CA MSs, and also by DA MSs when they are on a π/4-DQPSK or D8PSK assigned channel.
Under what condition should the Base Station not send SYSINFO-DA or SYNC-DA PDUs on an assigned channel?
If an assigned channel is shared by MSs from different DA cells, the BS should not send the SYSINFO-DA or SYNC-DA PDU on that assigned channel.
What is the purpose of general network broadcast PDUs sent by the SwMI at the MLE level regarding neighbour cells?
The purpose is to provide information about neighbour cells to aid the MS in making choices about cell reselection.
What specific information does a SwMI include in general network broadcast PDUs when it supports non-conforming channels?

The information includes the modulation modes and RF bandwidths of the available channel classes and irregular channels, the BS ERPs of the channel classes, and the frequencies of the irregular channels.
How does the MS MLE utilize the information about channel classes and irregular channels provided by a SwMI supporting non-conforming channels?

The MS MLE uses this information to assess the quality of the available channel classes and/or channels via measurements and path loss calculations performed by the MAC, and to provide channel selection advice to the SwMI.
How are SYNC-DA PDU and SYSINFO-DA PDU transmitted on a DA main carrier?
On a DA main carrier, the SYNC-DA PDU and SYSINFO-DA PDU are transmitted in frame 18 using a fixed mapping.
Under what conditions can SYNC-DA PDU and SYSINFO-DA PDU be transmitted on QAM channels?
The SYNC-DA PDU and SYSINFO-DA PDU (and SYSINFO-Q PDU) may be transmitted at any time on any QAM channel.
Why is the transmission rule for SYNC-DA PDU on QAM channels different from that of SYNC PDU on phase modulation channels?
On a QAM channel, the SICH-Q/D indicates whether each QAM downlink burst is an FCB, which contains the SYNC-DA PDU.
What information does an MS obtain from decoding the SYNC PDU after acquiring synchronization with a CA cell?
The MS obtains the MNI and colour code to de-scramble other bursts, as well as the slot, frame, and multiframe number to achieve full frame synchronization with the BS.
What is the first step for an MS wishing to synchronize with a DA cell?
The MS first attempts to synchronize with the QAM Frequency Correction Burst (FCB).
What information is contained in the SYNC-DA PDU that allows the MS to de-scramble other bursts from the BS?
The SYNC-DA PDU contains the MNI and colour code, which are used by the MS to de-scramble the contents of all other bursts transmitted by that BS.
After decoding the SYNC and SYSI NFO PDUs, how does the MS locate the MCCH?
The MS locates the MCCH on slot 1 of the main carrier or the appropriate common SCCH.
What capabilities does the MS gain after decoding both the SYNC-DA and SYSI NFO-DA PDUs?
The MS can locate the MCCH-Q or the appropriate QAM common SCCH, receive other downlink PDUs, and transmit uplink PDUs when permitted by usual reception and transmission procedures.
What is the difference in decoding requirements for subsequent SYNC-DA and SYSI NFO-DA PDUs while the MS is camped on a cell?
While camped on the cell, the MS must continue to decode subsequent SYSI NFO-DA PDUs, but continuing to decode subsequent SYNC-DA PDUs is optional.
Under what condition must the MS seek a new cell?
The MS has to seek a new cell when the main carrier on the current serving cell fails to achieve certain defined signal level criteria.
How does the MS estimate the performance of the main carrier when not receiving a conforming channel on a non-conforming concentric or sectored channel?
The MS estimates the performance by applying BS Effective Radiated Power (ERP) and other conversion factors to measurements on the current channel.
Which channel types may have lower radial ranges than the main carrier and potentially fail to fully cover its area?
Concentric channels and fully super-sectored channels may have lower radial ranges than the main carrier, meaning they do not necessarily fully cover the area covered by the main carrier.
How are sectored, semi-super-sectored, and eccentric channels classified regarding irregularity?
Sectored channels and semi-super-sectored channels are always irregular channels, while eccentric channels may be irregular channels.
What information must the MS MLE provide to the SwMI when requesting permission for a PDP context on non-conforming concentric or fully super-sectored channels?
For non-conforming concentric channels and fully super-sectored channels, it is sufficient for the MS MLE to tell the SwMI which channel classes it can use, without identifying individual channels.
How does an MS estimate signal levels for different channel classes compared to investigating signal levels on an irregular channel?

The MS estimates expected signal levels for different channel classes by applying conversion factors to measurements made on the current channel or the main carrier. In contrast, it investigates the signal level on an irregular channel by making direct signal level measurements on that specific irregular channel.
